title: The Hidden Look-Ahead: Point-in-Time Leakage in Electricity Market Data

primary_sources.paraphrase: arXiv record (v1, 2026-10-18, cs.LG, one author, CC BY 4.0): 128,656 forecast runs from ten weather-model configurations matched to two GB auction gates, 2022-2026; the latest-issued-before-gate rule picks an unpublished run on over 99% of days for six configurations at one gate; apparent accuracy gain -9% to +24%. No code or data link.

Full text: one commercial archive with issue, publication and finalisation times; vendor wind, solar and demand forecasts for GB; leakage shares per configuration, gate and clock season; MAE-based gain of naive over finalisation-rule selection on 882 days with 95% bootstrap intervals; eight-step audit protocol; no model fitted, no code or data statement.

claims.text: Selecting the latest run issued before the gate picks a run not yet published at the gate on more than 99% of delivery days for six of the ten weather-model configurations, at one of the two gates.
claims.metric: configurations (of 10) with over 99% of delivery days leaked at one gate
claims.dataset: Energy Quantified archive, GB, 128,656 runs, 1,734 delivery days 2022-01-01 to 2026-09-30
claims.horizon: GB day-ahead (09:50) and first intraday (17:30) auction gates, day before delivery

claims.text: For GFS at the day-ahead gate the naive rule picks an unpublished run on 99.8% of summer (BST) delivery days.
claims.metric: share of delivery days with an unpublished run selected (%)
claims.dataset: Energy Quantified archive, GB, GFS-driven forecasts, summer-clock days

claims.text: For GFS at the day-ahead gate the same share is 0.6% of winter (GMT) delivery days.
claims.metric: share of delivery days with an unpublished run selected (%)
claims.dataset: Energy Quantified archive, GB, GFS-driven forecasts, winter-clock days

claims.text: The apparent accuracy gain of the leaking selection is at its lowest about -9%: GFS-driven demand forecasts at the intraday gate in summer (-8.6%), where the leaked run looks worse.
claims.metric: apparent MAE gain of naive over finalisation-rule selection (%)
claims.dataset: Vendor GB demand forecasts vs vendor outturns, summer days within 2024-01-01 to 2026-05-31
claims.horizon: first intraday gate; lead time of compared values not stated
claims.baseline: run selected by the finalisation rule at zero margin

claims.text: The gain is at its highest about +24%: ICON-driven demand forecasts at the day-ahead gate in summer (24.2%).
claims.metric: apparent MAE gain of naive over finalisation-rule selection (%)
claims.dataset: Vendor GB demand forecasts vs vendor outturns, summer days within 2024-01-01 to 2026-05-31
claims.horizon: day-ahead gate; lead time of compared values not stated
claims.baseline: run selected by the finalisation rule at zero margin

claims.text: Over all days, GFS-driven demand forecasts at the day-ahead gate look 17.9% more accurate under the leaking selection (95% interval 16.2 to 19.7).
claims.metric: apparent MAE gain of naive over finalisation-rule selection (%)
claims.dataset: Vendor GB demand forecasts vs vendor outturns, 882 delivery days 2024-01-01 to 2026-05-31
claims.horizon: day-ahead gate; lead time of compared values not stated
claims.baseline: run selected by the finalisation rule at zero margin

claims.text: Over all days, GFS-driven demand forecasts at the intraday gate look 4.6% less accurate under the leaking selection (95% interval -5.8 to -3.4).
claims.metric: apparent MAE gain of naive over finalisation-rule selection (%)

claims.metric: added forecast age from a 5-minute margin (hours)

relevance.rationale: An audit of input timing, not a forecasting method. The series are a vendor's half-hourly GB wind, solar and demand forecasts used as inputs to price studies; demand is one of three and no load model is built, so 2 rather than 3. The decision points are the day-ahead and first intraday auction gates (2); the lead time of the compared values is not stated. The inputs are weather-model-driven forecasts treated as known-future covariates, but not temperature itself (2). Its relevance to us is to hard rule 2 and the forecast regime: issue time is not availability time, the point protocol.yaml already records as publication_latency_caveat.

checks.notes: Central model: none. The paper fits no price or load model and names no pretrained model, so there are no weights and no date to compare with the scored window; training_overlap_risk is unknown for that reason, and licence is null (the write-up itself is CC BY 4.0). Pre-registration: none stated in the full text. Replication: two searches (code or data by the author; replication or citation of the arXiv id) found nothing, so unknown; the paper is a five-week-old single-author v1 preprint. Evidence strength weak: the window is long (1,734 delivery days for the timing shares, 882 for the accuracy comparison) and the accuracy table carries bootstrap intervals, but there is no code and the data are a commercial archive, so nothing can be re-derived; spec's 'numbers without code or data'. The paper's intervals are 95% (7-day block bootstrap, 2,000 resamples), not 90%, so ci90 is null and the intervals are given in the claim text. Inconsistency found, not resolved: the abstract's 'six of ten' is never derived in the body; the leakage table is split by summer and winter clock with no all-days column, and nine configurations pass 99% in at least one season-and-gate cell. Weighting the two seasons by their days does give six (ICON-SR, ECMWF-SR, ECMWF-SR-ENS, ECMWF-ENS, AIFS, AIFS-ENS), but that is an inference made while reading, not the paper's statement; two of the six (AIFS) cover 2026 only. The abstract's -9% and +24% are summer-only cells of the demand rows; the all-days range in the same table is about -5% to +18%. Not verified: the table values themselves (read through a summarising fetch of the arXiv HTML, not the PDF or TeX source); what the vendor's publication and finalisation timestamps mean (the author says the documentation is minimal and relies on delay regularity and a one-evening live poll of three runs); the outturns, which are revised and from the same vendor; the lead time of the values compared. The accuracy gain is about the vendor's input forecasts, not about any downstream forecast: the author leaves the effect on predictive performance unmeasured. Bearing on our benchmark, not measured here: our forecast regime uses Open-Meteo Previous Runs matched by lead, and protocol.yaml already states that a run started shortly before the cutoff may not have been public at it. The paper's median publication delays (2.75 to 6.72 h after issue, from a different vendor) suggest the size of that exposure but do not transfer to Open-Meteo's best_match feed without a check of its own.

label: PARTIAL
label_reason: The paper is sourced and bears directly on our no-lookahead rule for the forecast weather regime, but it is a timing audit with no model, code or public data, so nothing in it can be run or re-measured on the PJM benchmark and its evidence is weak under the spec. Its headline count is not derived in the body and its accuracy effect concerns a vendor's input forecasts on GB price-auction gates, not week-ahead load error.
implementation_hint: Nothing to run: no model in runnable_models is involved and the data are a commercial archive. What could be taken from it is the audit idea, as work beyond an adapter and outside protocol-v1: record when each Open-Meteo run behind temperature_2m_previous_day{k} became public, compare with the Monday 00:00 America/New_York cutoff (converted to UTC per origin, so the offset changes with daylight saving), and report the share of origins and horizon hours affected. That would be a new check with its own DEVIATIONS.md line, not a change to the frozen protocol.
